answer: Choosing between two programs that both improve health requires comparing them head-to-head rather than each against doing nothing. A community health worker model and a digital health platform may differ in per-person cost, reach, and engagement, so the relevant question is which delivers more health for each dollar. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) between the two programs answers this by dividing the difference in their costs by the difference in their health effects. Because every dollar spent on one program cannot be spent elsewhere, the decision rests on opportunity cost, not on whether a program simply works.

faqs.q: How do you compare two health programs that both work?
faqs.a: Compute the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio between them by dividing the difference in cost by the difference in health effect, which shows which program delivers more health per dollar.

faqs.q: Why isn't it enough to know that a program works?
faqs.a: Many programs improve health. The economist's question is which program improves health the most for each dollar spent, because funding one means forgoing the next best use of those resources.

faqs.q: What tradeoffs distinguish a community health worker program from a digital health platform?
faqs.a: Community health workers reach people who avoid clinics but carry ongoing staffing costs, while a digital platform has lower per-person costs and broader reach but variable engagement and gaps in digital access.
